opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, because checking wasn't the point. When I asked the team to start using OpenClaude in their daily work, I wasn't trying to enforce a rule. I wanted to change how people think about their own work. If I had gone around checking who opened it and who didn't, it would have become a compliance task, and people would use it just to show they had used it. That's the worst outcome, because you get the behavior without the understanding.

What I cared about was whether people would really feel the difference themselves: that a model can now take on a meaningful part of research and engineering, and that your role shifts from doing every step by hand to defining problems, judging results, and steering. You can't force that realization. Someone has to hit a real problem, try the tool, and see it save them a day, or see it fail in an interesting way that teaches them something about where the models are.

There's also a practical reason. The people who are most curious and most driven try these things right away anyway, and they become the examples. Others see a colleague moving twice as fast and naturally follow. That kind of spread is much more durable than anything I could enforce from the top.

And frankly, in a research team, trust matters more than supervision. If I hire people I believe in, I should give them the direction and the reason behind it, and then let them decide how to get there. If someone has a good reason not to use it for a particular task, I'd rather hear that reason than have them pretend. So verifying felt unimportant. What mattered was whether the mindset changed, and that shows up in the work, not in a usage log.

r001.rationale: The response says colleagues may see others move faster and follow, but it does not explain that the instruction was intended to warn that people who did not use OpenClaude risked falling behind.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because the point was never compliance. When I told the team to use OpenClaude, I wasn't handing down a process rule that needed auditing. I was trying to change what people expected from their own workflow. If the tool is actually better, people migrate to it on their own within a week or two, because they feel the difference every day. If it isn't better, me checking a spreadsheet of who's using it doesn't make it better. It just adds friction and a bit of resentment.

There's also a cost to verifying. The moment a lead starts checking whether everyone followed an instruction, the message people hear is "the boss cares about obedience," not "the boss cares about results." I'd rather spend that attention on looking at the output. If someone ships great work with a different setup, fine. That tells me something useful too, maybe that our tooling has gaps I hadn't noticed.

And practically, in a small research team you see everything anyway. You see the pull requests, you see how fast someone iterates, you see what they paste into the group chat. You don't need a formal check to know who adopted it. So I just let it be an experiment: suggest it, give people the reasons, then watch what actually happens. Most of them switched. The few who didn't had reasons I ended up agreeing with.

r001.rationale: The response says people would adopt OpenClaude if they felt it improved their workflow, but it does not say that people who did not use it risked falling behind.

r001.rationale: The response says the instruction was meant to encourage people to try OpenClaude and assess its usefulness. It does not say that people who did not use it risked falling behind.
